en: The Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai of the Sui Dynasty spoke this, recorded by his disciple Guanding.
Next, the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) clarifies only the Single Truth of Reality (*ekasatyam*). As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "Reality is indeed the One Truth."
Thus he spoke of three;
now we follow this same principle.
In reality, there is but one truth, yet it is expediently taught as three.
The *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"Furthermore, by means of various other skillful means, one assists in manifesting the primary meaning.
This constitutes the characteristics of the inclusion and exclusion of the two truths, the three truths, and the single truth within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
Next, to clarify the separation and integration of the Four Truths:
while the first three truths— two truths and one truth— are all explained through vertical analysis,
the Four Truths are discussed through horizontal exposition.
Thus, there are four kinds of the Four Noble Truths:
namely, those with arising and ceasing, those without arising and ceasing, the immeasurable, and the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
The Four Noble Truths with arising and ceasing are precisely the horizontal exposition of the two truths of the Tripitaka.
The four truths of non-arising are the horizontal opening of the two truths of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
The immeasurable four truths are the horizontal opening of the two truths of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao).
The four truths of non-action are the horizontal opening of the single reality truth of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
Now, regarding the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, these four sets of the Four Noble Truths are integrated therein.
As the treatise says: "Phenomena produced through causes and conditions..."
This is the Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing;
what I teach is that they are empty.
This is the Four Noble Truths of non-arising.
This is also a provisional designation;
it is the immeasurable Four Noble Truths,
and it is also called the meaning of the Middle Way.
This refers precisely to the Four Noble Truths of Non-action.
Second, regarding the wisdom of discerning the distinctions between separation and integration,
as stated in various sutras:
Some say there is one wisdom, others two, three, four, or even up to eleven wisdoms and so forth.
If it is said that three wisdoms may be used to contemplate the three truths,
how should one contemplate them when they increase or decrease accordingly?
First, regarding the wise person:
the sutra states,
"All Tathāgatas share one and the same Dharma-body."
The one mind and the one wisdom,
as well as the powers and the fearlessnesses, are likewise so.
The single Buddha-wisdom is itself the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
To know all the various types of characteristics, modes, and appearances within the single characteristic of quiescence is called the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
This wisdom contemplates the three truths.
If one says that the single mark is the mark of quiescence,
this is precisely contemplating the Middle Way;
if one says that all various types of activities and characteristics are known, [this is likewise so].
This is precisely the simultaneous illumination of the two truths.
As for the two wisdoms, they are the provisional and the real.
The provisional consists of the knowledge of all modes and the knowledge of the paths.
Contemplating existence and non-existence refers to the two truths.
Reality—that is, the wisdom of all modes—refers to the contemplation of the middle-way truth.
It need not be explained that these three wisdoms contemplate the three truths, as this is already understood.
Regarding the four knowledges:

as clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dapin), they are the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñatā*), the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākāra-jñatā*), omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākāra-jñatā*).
The commentary provides several interpretations of these.
Alternatively, when within the causal stage there exists only the essence of principle,
it is termed the wisdom of the path and the wisdom of the aspects of the path; when, at the level of fruition, both phenomena and principle are fully perfected, [it is termed omniscience].
It is called "all-knowledge" (sarvajñā) and "knowledge of all modes" (sarvākārajñā).
Alternatively, it is said that because of the provisional and the real within the causal stage, they are termed "path-knowledge" (mārgajñā) and "knowledge of the paths of others" (mārgāntarajñā).
Entering into emptiness constitutes real wisdom, while entering into the conventional constitutes provisional wisdom.
Alternatively, it is said that because of the provisional and the real at the level of the fruit, they are termed "all-knowledge" (sarvajñatā) and "knowledge of all modes" (sarvākārajñatā).
Directly perceiving the Middle Way is called "all-knowledge" (sarvajñatā);
simultaneously illuminating the two truths is called "knowledge of all modes" (sarvākārajñatā).
Alternatively, it is said:
Regarding the general and specific aspects within the cause and the general and specific aspects upon the fruit,
some say that the wisdom of the path (*mārgajñatā*) and the wisdom of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) are the singular elucidations of the provisional and the real.
The "all-knowledge" (sarvajñatā) and the "knowledge of all modes" (sarvākārajñatā) further clarify the provisional and the real.
Through such various explanations, the four wisdoms are interpreted;
these four wisdoms are simply the illumination of the three truths.
If there are passages within the sūtras that clarify five, six, seven, eight, nine, or even an infinite number of truths,
one should simply grasp this underlying principle to interpret them so that they are subsumed within the three truths.
As for the eleven knowledges:
The two types of knowledge—worldly knowledge and knowledge of others' minds—illuminate conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Eight knowledges contemplate ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) contemplates the Middle Way.
This is called the wisdom that possesses both separation and union, while the three truths remain unmoved.
Furthermore, regarding the simultaneous opening of wisdom and the truths,
they mutually encompass one another according to their respective quantities.
Just as there are three knowledges corresponding to the three truths,
there are two knowledges corresponding to the two truths;
this meaning is easy to understand.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "neither the truths nor the knowledges are opened," this may also be understood as referring to one truth and one knowledge, neither increasing nor decreasing.
If wisdom, despite its opening and closing, is ultimately real wisdom, it is capable of manifesting the reality-substance.
Next, regarding the analysis by combining the truths and wisdoms:
according to the Tripiṭaka, the True Truth gives rise to one eye and one wisdom.
The conventional truth gives rise to one eye and one wisdom;
the two truths together give rise to one eye and one wisdom.
The wisdom-eye and the knowledge of all modes take the ultimate truth as their object.
The Dharma-eye and the Knowledge of the Modes of the Path take conventional truth as their object.
The Buddha-eye and the Knowledge of All Modes take both the ultimate and conventional truths as their objects together.
It is not that they simultaneously illuminate both; rather, it is only that they illuminate them sequentially, before and after.
In the Shared Teaching (Pāṭha-sādhāraṇa), the two eyes and two wisdoms arise from the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya),
while one eye and one wisdom arise from the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Both the knowledge of all things (sarvajñatā) and the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) take the ultimate truth as their common object.
The knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā) takes conventional truth as its object. If it were to connect [the paths] separately,
conventional truth would give rise to one eye and one wisdom.
The Truth gives rise to one eye and one wisdom;
by opening the Truth, the Middle emerges, giving rise to one eye and one wisdom.
Wisdom taking the Truth as its object is also like this.
In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), each of the three truths gives rise to one eye and one wisdom;
the same applies to the wisdom that takes the truths as its object.
If the Separate Teaching were to employ two truths, [the same principle would apply].
Within the conventional, one eye and one wisdom arise suddenly;
within the conventional, one eye and one wisdom arise.
Within the ultimate truth, one eye and one wisdom arise.
The same applies to wisdom taking the truths as its object.
In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), the single Truth of Reality gives rise to the three eyes and the three wisdoms.
The same applies to wisdom taking the truths as its object.
Question:
How does the distinct [vehicle] connect with the [Mahāyāna]? Answer:
Once the delusions regarding the ultimate and the conventional have been exhausted through the initial two contemplations of emptiness and the provisional,
one then hears of the Middle Way;
yet, one must still cultivate contemplation to destroy ignorance.
One is able to manifest Buddhahood through the eight aspects.
This Buddha is the fruit, while the preceding two contemplations serve as the cause;
therefore, it is said that the distinct [path] connects to the shared [path].
This Buddha-fruit does not connect with the causes for the marks produced over three asaṃkhyeya kalpas and a hundred kalpas;
therefore, it does not connect with the Tripiṭaka.
Nor does it take this fruit to connect with the causes of the ten stages (bhūmi).
Therefore, it does not connect with the distinct [teachings].
It does not take this fruit to connect with the severance of ignorance in the ten abodes;
therefore, it does not connect with the perfect [teaching].
One can only attain the transition by means of the distinct [attainment];
such is the meaning. Fourth, to clarify gain and loss:
To lose it is to engage in conceptual deliberation; to attain it is the inconceivable.
If one says that wisdom arises from the mind and naturally illuminates objects, like a torch illuminating things, [this is merely a conventional description].
Whether illuminating or not illuminating, this thing is inherently present;
whether observing or not observing, the object is naturally so.
Thus, ultimate truth and wisdom do not depend upon one another.
If one says that cognition is not cognition in itself but becomes cognition by virtue of an object,
and that an object is not an object in itself but becomes an object by virtue of cognition—
just as length and shortness exist in mutual dependence.
This is a case of mutual dependence.
If one says that an object is not an object by itself, nor does it become an object through cognition,
then it is an object because of the causal conditions consisting of both the object and cognition.
Wisdom is likewise the same by analogy.
This is a case of obtaining a name through common conjunction.
If one were to say that all [phenomena] are not like the three aforementioned types, but are merely spontaneous (*svarasena*), [that would be incorrect].
This would mean that both object and cognition are without causes.
All four of these interpretations are flawed. Why is this so?
When there are the four clingings, there is dependence;
dependence is right and wrong;
right and wrong give rise to attachment and aversion; from attachment and aversion, all afflictions arise.
Because afflictions arise, conceptual proliferation and contention arise.
Because contention arises, the actions of body, speech, and mind are produced.
Because these actions are produced, one wanders in the ocean of suffering of saṃsāra with no prospect of liberation.
One should know that the four types of grasping are the root of birth and death;
therefore, Nāgārjuna cut them down.
All phenomena do not arise from themselves.
How can there be cognition of its own object?
There is no arising from another.
How can there be cognition of an object through mutual dependence?
There is no arising through coexistence.
How, then, could there be the conditions of object and cognition?
Nor is there arising without a cause.
How can one attain the natural state of境 (object) and 智 (wisdom)?
If one clings to the four views and remains attached,
with delusions and confusion entangling one another, how can this be called wisdom?
Now, by means of [the principle that things] do not arise from themselves and so forth, the four modes of arising are refuted.
Since these modes are refuted, there is no dependence, nor even karma and suffering;
when the pure mind is constantly unified, one is then able to perceive Prajñā.
For this reason, the suffering of the cognition of its own object does not arise;
that is to say, its arising cannot be described as "arising.
Therefore, Śāriputra remained silent.
Ultimately, when there is no causal object, neither cognition nor suffering arises;
this is precisely the "non-arising of non-arising," which is ineffable.
Therefore, Vimalakīrti remained silent.
The path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished;
although it cannot be spoken of, it can nevertheless be described by way of the four *siddhāntas*.
Alternatively, it is said that objects and cognition arise from themselves.
Even up to the point where some may speak of object and cognition as being without cause,
although they may formulate these four [theories], their attachment to intrinsic nature has long since been refuted,
as previously explained.
There are only names; names have no intrinsic nature.
These characters, being devoid of intrinsic nature, do not abide.
Nor does it abide;
this is what is called inconceivable.
Thus, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* says:
This refers to the meaning that the realm of inconceivable wisdom is illuminated by inconceivable wisdom.
It is the same as when one refutes the four modes of existence regarding both object and cognition.
This is called true wisdom (*bhūtaprajñā*).
If one teaches the knowledge of the four objects according to conditions through the four *siddhāntas*,
this is called provisional wisdom (*upāyaprajñā*).
In this way, ordinary beings lose both the object and the wisdom;
those of the two vehicles gain one and lose one;
and bodhisattvas gain both.
Why is this? Ordinary persons have the fault of acting according to their own nature, which lacks the four *siddhāntas*;
they have the fault of transforming others, which lacks the four *siddhāntas*.
The followers of the Two Vehicles destroy the four modes of being to enter the ultimate truth;
they regard their own practice as attainment,
yet fail to deliver sentient beings, which they consider a deficiency in transforming others.
The Bodhisattva is fully endowed with both;
therefore, they attain both.
Furthermore, the ordinary person loses both.
This is the fault of conceptualization.
For the two vehicles, one attains while the other fails;
both are products of conceptualization.
The Bodhisattva attains both;
both are inconceivable.
This is explained in terms of gain and loss according to the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
If viewed separately, both the Shared Teaching (tongjiao) and the Distinct Teaching (biejiao) possess these two attainments;
both are products of discursive thought.
Regarding the two attainments of the Distinct Teaching:
Both are inconceivable. If one considers the Perfect [Teaching] in relation to the Distinct [Teaching],
both the teaching and the path of the Distinct Teaching are attained.
Both are within the realm of conceptual thought.
Why is this? Because they are the skillful means of the teaching’s gateway.
Some say that ignorance gives rise to all phenomena;
some say that the dharma-nature gives rise to all phenomena;
and some say that through the cultivation of conditions, one manifests true cultivation.
Some say that the truth is self-manifesting;
yet by clinging to this, one again incurs the fault of [reifying] nature and falls into the realm of the conceivable.
If one realizes the Way, it is precisely the inconceivable.
If the teaching and realization of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) are both inconceivable,
why is this so? Because the ultimate truth is beyond words, the four types of teaching are established for the sake of conditions.
There is only a provisional name;
the name of this provisional name is itself unborn.
Therefore, both scripture and realization are inconceivable.
Because there is no thought and no recollection, there is no dependence on conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) or the karma of fetters.
Because there is no karma, there is no birth and death.
This is called attaining the realization through one's own practice.
Having attained the true essence (*tattva*), one is able to use the ineffable to teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to transcend birth and death and attain the true essence.
This is what is meant by both self and others attaining the essence. Fourth, the clarification of the inclusion of dharmas (*dharmasaṃgraha*):
Those who harbor doubts claim that the names "calm abiding" (śamatha) and "insight" (vipaśyanā) are abbreviated and do not comprehensively encompass all phenomena. This is not so;
calm abiding and insight are total retainers (dhāraṇī) that universally include all phenomena.
Why is this? *Śamatha* (calm abiding) can pacify all phenomena;
it is like cauterizing a disease at its precise point, whereby all ailments are eliminated.
Contemplation can illuminate the principle; like obtaining the king of jewels, one acquires all treasures and becomes fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* contains one hundred and twenty sections as well as all dharmas.
All say that one should study Prajñā;
Prajñā is simply the wisdom of contemplation.
This wisdom of contemplation already encompasses all dharmas.
Furthermore, this King Samādhi is such that all samādhis enter into it.
Now, to discuss more extensively the inclusion of dharmas, there are six points.
First, it encompasses all principles;
second, it encompasses all delusions;
third, it encompasses all wisdom.
Fourth, it encompasses all practices;
fifth, it encompasses all stages;
sixth, it encompasses all teachings.
Regarding this sequence of six:
whether a Buddha appears or not, the rational nature (dharmatā) is eternally present.
Due to delusion regarding this principle, the afflictions of birth and death arise.
Observing in accordance with principle, one therefore discusses wisdom (*jñāna*);
through understanding, one establishes practice; by means of practice, one realizes the stages (*bhūmi*);
and because the stages are fulfilled, one teaches others.
The sequence of phenomena, principles, understanding, practice, cause and effect, self and others, and so forth,
is entirely subsumed within śamatha and vipaśyanā.
○ First, regarding how the three types of śamatha and the three types of vipaśyanā subsume all principles:
The principle is the Dharma of Truth; as explained above, its various combinations and distinctions differ according to whether they are partial or perfect.
Apart from the provisional and the real, there is no other separate principle.
Aside from Mount Malaya, there is no sandalwood elsewhere.
If there were anything further, it would be false speech.
Since the essence is revealed through śamatha and vipaśyanā,
it encompasses all principles.
Second, regarding how śamatha and vipaśyanā subsume all delusions:
because one is deluded regarding the truths, the delusions of saṃsāra arise;
this delusion is precisely ignorance (avidyā).
If one is deluded regarding the provisional principle, there arise the ignorance associated with the realm and the independent ignorance;
that which is conjoined with the various proclivities of views and afflictions is termed "associated."
That which is dissociated is called "independent.
Because one does not know this matter, greed arises;
this lack of knowledge is ignorance (*avidyā*).
The arising of craving is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Craving is consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Consciousness arising together with the four aggregates is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
The movement of the various faculties toward form is the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
That which is clung to by the six sense bases is contact (*sparśa*).
Contact that accords with sensory objects is feeling (*vedanā*).
That which experiences what is pleasant and desired is craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
The entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) co-arising with craving are grasping (*upādāna*).
The karma that produces future birth is becoming (*bhava*).
The arising of future aggregates is birth;
the maturation of the aggregates is old age;
the discarding of the aggregates is death.
These twelve wheels function as mutual causes and effects:
afflictions pervade karma,
and karma pervades suffering.
Because suffering pervades the afflictions,
it is called the "three paths.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
The former practices are included within the latter three;
the latter practices are included within the former seven.
These seven are both karma and the path.
They are able to lead one through to future lives.
Although the latter three are not themselves karma, they are able to lead through the seven; thus they also constitute this path.
In the sūtras, they are also called the twelve links (*dvādaśa-aṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) or the twelve wheels (*dvādaśa-cakra*).
Because its bondage is inexhaustible, it is called a "wheel" (*cakra*).
Because the three periods of time are partitioned, it is called "segmented.
It obscures the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), preventing one from attaining liberation.
This is precisely the sickness; by speaking of the sickness, one knows the medicine.
The medicine consists of the śamatha and vipaśyanā that proceed from the conventional into emptiness.
By contemplating the medicine, one knows the sickness.
Therefore, these delusions are subsumed within the śamatha and vipaśyanā that enter into emptiness.
If one is deluded regarding the true principle, there arise the ignorance associated with the realms beyond, as well as independent ignorance. Why is this so?
Although the associated and independent [afflictions] within the realm have been severed, their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) still remain.
In the Hīnayāna, these tendencies are not considered primary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*);
however, according to the definitive teaching of the Mahāyāna, the tendencies are themselves distinct afflictions.
This refers to ignorance that lies outside of this realm.
Therefore, the *Ratnagotravibhāga* states:
"Although those of the two vehicles possess the remedies of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, selflessness, and so forth..."
Regarding the Buddha’s Dharma-body, this is still a perversion.
This perversion is precisely ignorance acting independently.
The activity of untainted wisdom constitutes the three kinds of mind-made bodies.
These are also the five kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*).
"Mind" refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*);
"body" refers to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*).

The fact that ignorance, subtle afflictions, and conceptual proliferation have not yet been completely extinguished is precisely the non-termination of the defilement of craving and grasping, the defilement of karma, and the defilement of birth;
this is precisely "existence" (bhava).
The three types of mental causes that shift constitute birth;
the transformation of their fruit constitutes old age and death.
These twelve factors collectively constitute the four kinds of obstacles within the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
This refers to the arising and destruction conditioned by signs.
"Conditions" (pratyaya) refer to the path of afflictions;
"signs" (nimitta) refer to the path of karma.
Birth and destruction are themselves the path of suffering;
therefore, one knows that the twelve links of dependent origination exist outside the realms. Why is this so?
From the point of descending as a Buddha downward, all possess ignorance (*avidyā*).
Since karma is moistened by ignorance, and once karma has been so moistened, how could there be no suffering?
Although these twelve links of dependent origination do not regress to the higher realms, they fall into the lower ones.
It is permissible to proceed from the wheel of ignorance to old age and death,
and from the wheel of old age and death back to ignorance;
for it is precisely due to these afflictions that one is obstructed from the true principle.
These delusions are the objects to be remedied by both the contemplation of the conventional and the contemplation of the middle way.
To further analyze this: why is that so?
There are generally many types of the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*).
If one distinguishes between the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) and the bodhisattvas who have attained mastery,
those who have previously severed all afflictions within the realm of desire and eliminated them completely [attain the first type].
However, those who have never practiced the provisional middle way are born outside the realms;
since the afflictions outside the realms have not been suppressed at all, their faculties are dull.
When practicing contemplation upon those [dharmas],
one must necessarily undergo sequential cultivation and training throughout kalpas to learn the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
first shattering the "dust-like sands" [of afflictions].
Although the dust-like [afflictions] do not moisten rebirth, they can obstruct the path of transformation; therefore, they must be severed first.
As for those who sever these delusions:
Calm abiding (śamatha) is the skillful means for taming the mind;
it subdues the afflictions outside the realms [of existence].
Through exertion (pragraha), one severs the three paths [of karma], as well as the associated and independent secondary and primary branches, all of which are eliminated.
Therefore, one knows that the provisional contemplation correctly subsumes the dust-like afflictions (*rajas*) and also subsumes ignorance (*avidyā*). If,
for those of the Separate and Perfect [vehicles], the delusions common to both vehicles have been exhausted and the delusions specific to their own vehicle have been suppressed;
Those born in that realm possess sharp spiritual faculties;
they simply cultivate the Middle Way to treat those three paths,
from the first bhūmi through to the final bhūmi.
Within each stage there are three paths:
the extinction of ignorance in each stage leads to the extinction of karma, which in turn leads to the extinction of suffering.
As one proceeds through each stage [bhūmi], even when proceeding alone, one likewise proceeds.
Although wisdom exists within each stage, it is mixed with ignorance;
because of this mixture, it may also be termed an "obstruction to wisdom" (jñeyāvaraṇa).
Because it obstructs the higher-stage knowledge,
when there is no ignorance within the mind of a Buddha alone, the path of afflictions is exhausted.
Because the path of afflictions is exhausted, karma is exhausted.
Because karma is exhausted, suffering is exhausted.
The ultimate culmination of the three paths resides solely in the Tathāgata.
Therefore, Madhyamaka encompasses the afflictions beyond the [three] realms.
Regarding the third point, that the three types of śamatha-vipaśyanā encompass all wisdoms:
the various wisdoms, whether categorized separately or combined as previously explained,
are all fully and exhaustively subsumed within these three contemplations.
Conventional wisdom that does not illuminate the principle is already subsumed within the eleven knowledges;
if the twenty knowledges are explained in detail,
they are likewise subsumed under the three contemplations.
Fourth, regarding how śamatha and vipaśyanā encompass all practitioners:
the aforementioned wisdom is understanding;
yet, if there is understanding without practice, one will ultimately reach nothing.
There are two kinds of practice:
namely, the practice of wisdom and the practice of conduct.
As for the practice of wisdom and the practice of conduct within the Tripiṭaka:
Up to the point of the practice of wisdom and the practice of conduct within the circle:
the practice of wisdom is the primary practice,
while the practice of conduct is the auxiliary practice.
Vipassanā can destroy the afflictions;
furthermore, it requires the power of samatha to assist right knowledge and vision.
These two—primary and auxiliary practices—proceed in accordance with wisdom.
Just as the feet follow the eyes,
so too, within the Tripitaka, the analytical contemplation of impermanence is the practice of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*), while the contemplations of impurity,
loving-kindness, and so forth are the practice of conduct (*caryā-caryā*).
These two lines follow the analytical wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyā-jñāna*) to enter into emptiness.
If one understands that the essence of all phenomena is like an illusion or a magical transformation, this is the practice of wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*).

To practice *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* by means of counting the breaths, the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and taking various objects as conditions throughout all phenomena, is the practice of conduct (*caryā-caryā*).

These two lines follow the nature of the Dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) as it enters into emptiness. If, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, one cultivates the Path-knowledge (mārga-jñāna), its engagement with conventional principles belongs to the category of wisdom-practice (prajñā-caryā);
its engagement with conventional phenomena belongs to the category of conduct-practice (caryā-caryā).
These two lines follow the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgajñatā) in entering the conventional.
If the middle way takes the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) as its object,
this single path of purity is the practice of wisdom (prajñācaryā).
All the various dharma-gates and perfections traversed are the Mahāyāna.
The twelve links of dependent origination are themselves the Buddha-nature.
The foundations of mindfulness and so forth are the practices of cultivation.
These two lines follow middle wisdom (*madhyama-prajñā*) to enter into the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Furthermore, because the fundamental four dhyānas are equal in concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), they are subsumed under both.
The desire-realm concentration (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*) has little concentration and much wisdom, and is thus subsumed under insight (*vipaśyanā*).
The intermediate state is likewise.
The four formless absorptions (ārūpya-samāpatti) involve much wisdom and little tranquility, and are thus categorized under insight (vipaśyanā).
The first three of the four immeasurables (apramāṇa-citta) are categorized under insight.
The mind of equanimity is subsumed under the cessation [of perception and feeling]. The nine perceptions, the eight recollections, and the ten perceptions are subsumed under the contemplations.
The eight liberations are subsumed under the first three liberations as contemplations.
The latter five are subsumed under *śamatha* (calm abiding).
The nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), the lion’s stretch (*siṃhavijṛmbhita*), the leap (*vyutkrāntaka*), and so forth, are subsumed under *śamatha*.

nor hear others speak, and thus cannot know it,
so it is with an Arhat.
Since the Buddha-eye has not yet opened and one has not heard the Buddha’s teaching,
how could one know for oneself that [the nature] is eternally abiding?
Therefore, the Lotus Sūtra says:
Regarding the merit one has personally attained, one gives rise to the notion that it constitutes final nirvāṇa;
yet, if one encounters another Buddha, one then attains definitive understanding.
It is further said:
Neither Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, nor non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas can know it;
one should understand that they do not know it because they have not heard it. The Sūtra calls those who know it "those who equally know their own principle, the True Truth, and the Unconditioned."
Furthermore, it is eternally of a single, unchanging aspect.
If a person discriminates between two aspects of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and allows them to fluctuate,
they will be unable to give rise to the realization of the truth.
One must contemplate emptiness in order to enter the untainted state (*anāsrava*).
For example, Subhūti contemplated emptiness,
while Kauṇḍinya realized the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Furthermore, regarding those who do not possess the full restraint:
if they can contemplate emptiness and attain the precepts concurrent with the Path,
this constitutes the possession of the complete precepts.
Therefore, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
"The true nature and characteristics of all phenomena are eternally abiding and unchanging;
even the followers of the Two Vehicles attain these, yet they are not called Buddhas."
Therefore, it is known that the term "eternal" (nitya) can be explained in this way.
If this explanation were not provided,
the Tripiṭaka would not state that the Mahāyāna is eternal.
How could a śrāvaka possibly possess the path-concomitant precepts (mārga-sahabhū-śīla) that constitute the requisites for a śrāvaka?
If this is the interpretation, there is no fault in the path-concomitant precepts; rather, it further enhances their excellence.
Furthermore, to explain by means of an illustration,
as it says in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*:
"Lust obstructs birth in the Brahma-heaven, let alone [attaining] Bodhi."
To be born in the Brahma Heaven, one must sever desire;
to attain Bodhi, one must sever the desires of the two extremes.
Although the term "desire" is the same, its meaning differs accordingly.
This principle is likewise:
one who wishes to enter the ultimate truth must know that the unconditioned is eternal and immutable.
When entering into the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), one also knows that it is eternally abiding, of a single mark, and unchanging.
One knows that while the discourse on "eternity" is the same, there is a difference between the Great and Small Vehicles.
Therefore, the *śamatha-vipaśyanā* of the Tripiṭaka does not contradict the sūtras, even though it does not know the perfect reality (*pariniṣpanna-tattva*).
The Śrīmālādevī-sūtra states:
"If one does not know the eternally abiding [nature],
all forms of taking refuge will fail to be accomplished."
How is this to be reconciled?
[The sūtra] seeks the root, stating that those who first engage in the practice of the three vehicles are not deluded regarding the Dharma.
If one takes the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) regarding the four foundations of mindfulness as the beginning, [how does this accord with the sūtra?]
This initial realization of the eternal nature of the True Truth gives rise to no sixty-two views;
through a mind free from attachment and dependence, the noble ones achieve perfection.
This explanation shares the same intent as the previous one.
If, in ancient times, there were those who were beginners,
they first gave rise to the bodhicitta and early on came to know the eternal abiding [of reality].
Fearing birth and death, they may regress from the Great Vehicle to take up the Small Vehicle;
such are Prince Dharmatāla and those bodhisattvas who regress within the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
From the very beginning, they have taken refuge in the Three Jewels of the Single Essence and cultivated the precepts and wholesome deeds.
There is the dharma of receiving, but no dharma of relinquishing.
Because the mind is inexhaustible, the precepts are also inexhaustible;
all wholesome precepts are perfumed by this.
For example, just as the great earth silently benefits trees so that their sprouts and shoots all reach fulfillment, the precepts of the Śrāvaka vehicle do not depart from the Bodhisattva precepts;
it is through the power of the Bodhisattva precepts that they are able to bring them to completion.
This is precisely that meaning.
If one does not understand permanence through the performance of the initial action,
then the three collections of scriptures, the taking of refuge, the precepts, and the *karmavācanā* rituals will all fail to be accomplished.
If one provides this interpretation,
there will be no contradiction between the meanings of the two scriptures,
the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna. *Mohe zhiguan*, Scroll Three, Part Two.
